catalog_quote: [p.26, §2.2.1] La sílaba consta de una consonante opcional y una vocal, (C)V, y lleva tono alto o tono bajo. El tono bajo no se marca. (Véase la sección 2.3.1.) [...] [p.27, §2.2.2] La palabra fonológica está integrada por una a ocho sílabas. [...] 2.3. Fonología suprasegmental. 2.3.1. El tono. Hay dos tonos fonemáticos, alto /V́/ y bajo /V̀/. Puede ocurrir más de un tono alto en la palabra fonológica. Las pocas palabras que ocurren sólo con tono bajo no tienen acento perceptible. /riká/ 'brazo' /ríka/ 'fruta' /jái/ 'tigre' /jaí/ 'especie de batata' /hoá/ 'pelo' /hóa/ 'selva' /ísika/ 'mosquitos' /isíka/ 'mico tití'. Se distinguen las palabras para partes del cuerpo de personas y de animales sólo por el tono. [...] [p.28] Al principio de la palabra fonológica, cuando una sílaba con tono bajo precede a una sílaba con tono alto, el tono bajo opcionalmente ocurre con deslizamiento suave poco ascendente, con alargamiento poco perceptible de la vocal: /gibó/ [...] 'pie'. Un deslizamiento decreciente con alargamiento poco perceptible de la vocal ocurre opcionalmente en una sílaba de tono alto al final de la palabra fonológica: /tũhá/ [...] 'rana'. Todas las palabras de una sílaba con tono alto tienden a deslizarse a tono bajo. La vocal se alarga un poco: /wí/ [...] 'casa'.

new_statements.translation: 2.3 Suprasegmental phonology. 2.3.1 Tone. There are two phonemic tones, high and low. More than one high tone may occur in the phonological word. The few words that occur with low tone only have no perceptible accent. riká 'arm' / ríka 'fruit', jái 'jaguar' / jaí 'kind of sweet potato', hoá 'hair' / hóa 'forest', ísika 'mosquitoes' / isíka 'titi monkey'. Words for body parts of persons and of animals are distinguished only by tone. [...] All monosyllabic high-tone words tend to glide down to low tone.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (94-pp image scan) and its. I rendered PDF pp.43-44 (book pp.27-28) and read the page images directly. Puede ocurrir más de un tono alto en la palabra fonológica. Las pocas palabras que ocurren sólo con tono bajo no tienen acento perceptible.' followed by the minimal pairs /riká/ 'brazo' ~ /ríka/ 'fruta', /jái/ 'tigre' ~ /jaí/ 'especie de batata', /hoá/ 'pelo' ~ /hóa/ 'selva', /ísika/ 'mosquitos' ~ /isíka/ 'mico tití', and 'Se distinguen las palabras para partes del cuerpo de personas y de animales sólo por el tono.' with the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Macuna is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language: every (C)V syllable bears lexical H or L, H placement is contrastive (minimal pairs differing only in which syllable is H) and a word may carry several H tones; the only remark on accent is that perceived prominence goes with H tone, so the rare all-L words have no perceptible accent. No positional stress rule is given anywhere in the sketch (the suprasegmental section covers only tone and nasality). The companion 1993 dictionary adds that the main difference among Macuna subgroups (clan-lects) is 'la posición del acento en las palabras', and Ardila 1995 reports that every Macuna word carries at least one high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with only low tone lack perceptible accent; monosyllabic H words glide to L; optional slight rise on an initial L syllable before H and optional fall on a word-final H syllable (p.28). Dictionary (1993, p.5): accent position differs between the six subgroups (ide, taboti jejea, emoa, roea, sʉroa, yiba).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'palabra fonológica' (1-8 syllables, root plus suffixes); examples are isolated citation forms and inflected verbs; tone written with acute accent in the phonology chapter only, practical orthography omits tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The Bosquejo and dictionary describe Macuna as spoken in Colombia (río Comeña, Piraparaná and Apaporis, Vaupés; c. 450 speakers), data from several clans (ide, yiba, roea, emoa, sʉroa, taboti jejea); the dictionary states the subgroups differ mainly in accent position, so any positional generalisation may be clan-lect specific. Glottocode macu1260 / ISO myy. Gomez-Imbert (2004) and Motta (2025) treat Makuna and Barasana-Eduria (bara1380, ISO bsn) as a dialect continuum; Brazilian 'Makuna/Yeba-masã' varieties are the same language.

sources.note: Phonology §2 (pp.24-30). §2.2.1: syllable (C)V carries high or low tone, low unmarked. §2.3 'Fonología suprasegmental' has only §2.3.1 'El tono' and §2.3.2 'La nasalidad' -- no separate stress section. §2.3.1 (p.27): two phonemic tones, high and low; more than one high tone may occur in the phonological word; 'las pocas palabras que ocurren sólo con tono bajo no tienen acento perceptible'; tonal minimal pairs (ríka 'fruta' vs riká 'brazo', ísika vs isíka) and human vs animal body-part terms distinguished only by tone; p.28: optional slight rise on initial L before H, optional fall on final H,…

sources.note: §III 'La altura tonal' (pp.124-128): the four Pirá-Paraná varieties (tatuyo, carapana, barasana, macuna) have two distinctive tone heights; Macuna monosyllables always carry high tone; 'En barasana y macuna toda palabra lleva por lo menos un tono alto; no se presenta el patrón bajo-bajo'; Macuna summary: succession of two highs rare, mid-low frequent on initial syllable, every word has at least one high tone, tonal contrasts distinguish lexical and grammatical meaning. Treats the language as tonal; no stress statement.
